title: What to Know Before Trying Reiki
h1: What to Know Before Trying Reiki
excerpt: Before a Reiki session, know that it is a spiritual practice, that evidence does not show it treats disease, and that it must not delay care.

quick_answer.question: What should you know before trying Reiki?
quick_answer.answer: Know that Reiki is a hand-placement practice based on a claimed energy, that research has not shown it treats health conditions, and that you should not delay medical care. Ask what it costs and what the practitioner will not do.

intro: A first session is easier to judge if you walk in with the public caution already in mind. Surprise is how mild comfort gets narrated as medicine.

sections.heading: What are you agreeing to?
sections.content:
You will likely lie down, clothed, while someone places hands on or near you in quiet. You may feel relaxed. The theory on offer is a universal energy. NCCIH says that theory's health claims are not clearly supported. Britannica can tell you the practice's modern Japanese background.

The neighboring page is [what Reiki is](/articles/what-is-reiki/). Treat that link as part of the argument, not as decoration.

sections.heading: What should you ask?
sections.content:
Trainings and fees vary. A certificate is a biography of courses, not a clinical license. Some practitioners mix in chakras or other systems. Ask which system you are getting. The research page is the longer caution.

A wider map lives at the [research page](/articles/what-research-says-about-reiki/). Dates and school names matter, because a recent American presentation is often described as if it had no date.

sections.heading: What outcome is reasonable?
sections.content:
Ask whether they will tell you to stop other treatment. Leave if the answer is yes. Do not send medical records you would not want in an ordinary appointment. You can decline and still have read the explanation.

If you want a narrower practical or comparative page, use [the Reiki topic](/topics/reiki/). You can understand the description without joining a group or buying a course.

sections.heading: What should a careful reader refuse?
sections.content:
Do not use Reiki for an emergency. Do not treat calm as proof of healing energy. Children and serious illness belong with licensed care first.

Readers in the United States often meet a simpler version of the same idea in a class, an app, or a short video. Name that simpler version instead of pretending it is the whole tradition. Traditional teaching, personal report, and research stay in separate sentences on this site. The [editorial policy](/editorial-policy/) is the rule. The [disclaimer](/disclaimer/) applies whenever a sentence leans toward health, safety, or a promised transformation. The [corrections](/corrections/) page is how to challenge a factual mistake. Name the school, the text, or the century whenever a sentence would otherwise float free of history. A reader may stop at the definition when that is all the question required.

key_takeaways: The session is quiet hand placement.
Evidence does not show clinical effectiveness.

faq.question: Do I need to believe for it to be allowed?
faq.answer: Belief is the practitioner's theory. You do not have to adopt it to understand the page or to decline a session.

faq.question: Is this a full guide?
faq.answer: No. It answers one question and points to the longer page. It is not personal instruction or medical advice.
